A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ORCA research. All 24 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including Appendices A–C, are readable. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable matching across the appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original Meta-world and Humanoid experiments, including benchmark returns, training curves, temporal-misalignment tests, and pretraining analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds multiple-demonstration, baseline, visual-encoder, image-policy, and runtime results.

M1.justification: Section 5.6 introduces a multiple-demonstration adaptation: compute ORCA rewards separately for each video and take their maximum at each timestep, as defined in Equation 7. The original single-video recurrence, reward, pretraining procedure, and Humanoid confidence scaling remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same ten Meta-world and four Humanoid tasks remain. v2 adds an image-observation policy condition on five existing Meta-world tasks, extending evaluation beyond v1's state-input policies. Increased demonstration counts are experimental-setting changes rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds two substantially different comparator families on five Meta-world tasks: adversarial imitation through GAIfO and language-conditioned rewards through LIV. Existing comparators remain. GAIfO receives state demonstrations and LIV receives text goals, so these additions broaden comparison scope without providing identical-input comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds protocols varying demonstration count and speed composition, visual backbones, and policy observation modality. Its latency experiment uses 100 rollouts per method, demonstration length 100, and learner lengths 100 and 300. The original training budgets and Table 3 hyperparameters remain unchanged; newly documented randomization does not establish a change to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Sections 5.6–5.8 and Appendices C.4–C.6 add substantial analyses of demonstration scaling, mixed-speed demonstrations, Meta-world encoder sensitivity, dependence on state versus image policy inputs, and runtime scaling. The earlier temporal-misalignment, pretraining, Humanoid encoder, and qualitative failure analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.1 newly states that training and evaluation seeds differ. This adds seed documentation without establishing additional runs. Existing three-run analyses and mean/standard-error reporting remain; the additional result tables continue that reporting practice rather than introducing significance tests or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in Tables 1–5 are unchanged. Figure 6 and Tables 6–9 add substantial results: ORCA reaches 1.10 normalized return with 20 same-speed demonstrations, the image-policy comparison reports 0.76, and 100-frame reward computation takes 56.9 ms. Additional baseline and encoder results also appear. These are newly reported comparisons and settings, not version-to-version improvements on the original tests.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 adds an O(T times demonstration length) runtime claim and a lower-bound comparison with methods requiring a full frame-distance matrix. The ordering and coverage propositions, Appendix A proofs, and counterexamples retain their substance. Explicit trajectory arguments added to reward notation do not change those proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and concluding account retain the same sequence-level ordered-coverage contribution and reported 4.5x/6.6x headline improvements. The added experiments support and extend evaluation without redefining these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of encoder dependence and possible reasons for GAIfO and LIV underperformance. Section 7 replaces v1's explicit failure condition involving unrealizable subgoals with a broader task-misspecification caveat, and replaces identifying realizable subgoals as future work with incorporating language subgoals. Existing temporal-ordering and pretraining explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents default object-position randomization and distinct training/evaluation seeds, identifies the added baselines' input differences, and supplies backbone sizes and timing-workload details. The abstract replaces the direct code-repository pointer with a project-website pointer; this does not establish a change in actual code availability. Most existing implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds a focused comparison with demonstration-conditioned policies requiring action labels, citing works such as Duan, Jain, and Palo and Johns. New references also support GAIfO, LIV, and encoder variability. The central positioning against frame-level optimal transport remains; publication and citation-year updates otherwise refer to retained works.

P1.justification: v2 adds an appendix contents list, moves implementation material from v1's C.1–C.3 into B.4–B.6, and separates additional results into reorganized subsections. Local wording, headings, and publication text are revised. The main narrative and most existing prose remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds the multiple-demonstration chart in Figure 6 and Tables 6–9 for the new comparisons. It expands captions, relocates and resizes existing figures and tables, and adjusts some diagram annotations. The established layouts and most existing graphical content are preserved.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's state-input policies and fixed Meta-world encoder through image-policy and backbone comparisons, while testing demonstration scaling and computational cost. These additions address important uncertainties about applicability and practical performance. The experiments remain on limited task subsets, some baseline inputs differ, and the revised limitations lose a specific failure caveat, but the broader empirical scrutiny provides a clear net quality improvement.
